title: What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: We continue to be the sole suppliers to our customer – A French OEM for the engines for their microcars.
epigraph.author: Greaves Cotton management, Q2 FY27 earnings call, 29 October 2026

web_blocks.text: Greaves reports its business in two ways, and you need both. The management view splits the group into three core segments (Energy Solutions, Mobility Solutions, Industrial Solutions) plus two investee businesses, Greaves Electric Mobility Limited (GEML) and Greaves Finance Limited (GFL) [4][1]. The statutory view follows Ind AS 108, the accounting rule that makes a company report segments the way its chief operating decision-maker reviews them; at Greaves that is the CEO and the CFO [6]. The statutory segments were reorganised in Q2 FY27: Cables & Control Levers moved into Engines & Engineering Products and Vehicle Finance was split out [2]. The filings give EBITDA (operating profit before interest, tax and depreciation) for the core as a whole, not for Energy, Mobility or Industrial separately [1][2].

web_blocks.caption: Management view: revenue by segment (₹ crore), with growth and the main products and buyers
headers: What it sells, and to whom
rows: Diesel gensets of 5-2,500 kVA, spares and service; dealers and institutional buyers [4][1][43]
Three-wheeler and microcar engines, Excel cables, aftermarket parts, engineering services [4][1]
Fire-pump, farm, marine and small construction engines [4][1]
Core EBITDA ₹383 crore (14.4%) in FY26; ₹178 crore (12.0%) in H1 FY27 [4][1]
Ampere electric scooters; MLR Auto L5 three-wheelers [4][1][6]
Loans for electric vehicles, brand ev.fin [4][1][6]
web_blocks.takeaway: Mobility is the largest segment, with about 59% of FY26 core revenue, but it is not one business. Industrial's -5% in H1 FY27 hides +9% like-for-like once the exited farm-equipment machines are stripped out [1]. GEML's revenue doubled in H1 FY27, so the investees, which lose money, are growing faster than the core that earns the profit [1][2].

web_blocks.text: Of H1 FY27's ₹890 crore of Mobility revenue, ₹723 crore is Greaves's own engines, retail aftermarket and e-powertrain, ₹142 crore is Excel and ₹25 crore is Greaves Technologies, the engineering-services arm [1]. Diesel engines for three-wheeler makers (OEMs, original equipment manufacturers) brought in ₹545 crore in FY26, 15.8% of group revenue [3], and about 42% of Mobility in H1 FY27 [1]. In Energy, the medium-horsepower (MHP) gensets of 160-750 kVA grew 35% to ₹230 crore in H1 FY27 against the segment's 28%, and aftermarket sales of spares and service were ₹77 crore, up 15% [1]. Management puts its genset market share near 4% [30][29] and expects the market to grow 10-12% a year [27]. A genset is a diesel engine coupled to an alternator that makes electricity when the grid fails.

web_blocks.caption: Statutory view (Ind AS 108, before the Q2 FY27 reorganisation): FY26 revenue and segment result (₹ crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Engines earned ₹376.59 crore of result, 87.5% of the ₹430.34 crore made by the two profitable segments, while the electric segment lost ₹182.01 crore. These results are before ₹85.78 crore of central costs and ₹26.05 crore of finance cost. After other income and a ₹39.34 crore exceptional charge, profit before tax was ₹114.91 crore and, after ₹79.62 crore of tax, profit was ₹35.29 crore [6]. Percentages are our arithmetic on the cited figures.

web_blocks.text: After the reorganisation, Engines & Engineering Products had FY26 revenue of ₹2,554.74 crore and result of ₹416.52 crore (16.3%) [2]. Its H1 FY27 revenue of ₹1,478.05 crore equals the core revenue in the investor deck, which ties the two views together [2][1]. The filings do not reconcile the FY26 figure to the core's ₹2,665 crore.

web_blocks.caption: Recast statutory segments, FY26 and H1 FY27 (₹ crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: The first row is the one to watch. A year earlier, H1 FY26 revenue was ₹1,232.96 crore and result ₹209.67 crore (17.0%). Result barely moved on 20% more revenue, which matches the core EBITDA margin falling from 14.9% to 12.0% as input costs rose [2][1]. Vehicle Finance assets grew from ₹309.65 crore to ₹516.85 crore in six months as the loan book expanded [2].

web_blocks.text: Geography is thin. The statutory note splits revenue only into domestic and overseas: overseas was ₹343.93 crore in FY26, 10.0% of the total, up 72.7% from ₹199.19 crore (6.8%) [6]. Management's own “international” measure is 13% of core revenue in both FY26 and H1 FY27, up from 9% in FY25; the two measures differ because one uses core revenue and the other the whole group, investees included [6][1]. Exports include Euro V+ engines for European microcars, Excel parts for OEMs in Europe, the US and Asia, gensets for the Middle East, Africa and Nepal, and fire-engine exports that began in Q1 FY27 [6][24][25]. Mobility exports fell 4% to ₹106 crore in H1 FY27 while domestic sales grew [1].

web_blocks.title: Example 1, Energy Solutions: a 250 kVA genset for a factory or clinic
paragraphs: The buyer is a manufacturing plant, IT park, clinic, bank, petrol station or railway site that cannot stop when the grid trips; the product page lists these uses [46]. kVA measures electrical capacity, so 250 kVA is about 200 kW. Management says demand has moved “from addressing basic power deficits to prioritising uptime and operational continuity” [6]. The product is model GPWII-PIV-250C: 415 volts, three-phase, a 385-litre fuel tank, 3,110 kg dry weight, an enclosure rated for 50°C and compliance with the CPCB IV+ emission rules for gensets [46].

Engines for small and medium sets are made in-house; for the highest horsepower a strategic partner supplies the engine, and management says its data-centre play is “limited” [26][24]. Assembly is at Talegaon near Pune, with engines from the CSN plants [6]. No list price is published; buyers are sent to a dealer [46]. Sales go through “3S Composite Dealers” (sales, service and spares) and direct institutional orders, with a five-year extended warranty available [46][6].

The money continues after the sale. A turnkey option covers site preparation, installation and commissioning [43]. The largest single order to date, ₹35 crore in Q4 FY26, bundles supply, installation, commissioning and long-term maintenance [26]. Aftermarket grew 35% in FY26 against 20% for the segment [4].

web_blocks.title: Example 2, Mobility Solutions: the engine inside a three-wheeler or a French microcar
paragraphs: A three-wheeler maker needs a low-cost, durable engine that meets the BS-VI emission standard and costs little to run. A European microcar maker needs a Euro V+ diesel for its small quadricycles. Greaves does not name its Indian OEM customers; the one named is Ligier, the French microcar maker, for which Greaves is the sole engine supplier [1][62]. The company says it is the largest maker of single-cylinder diesel engines, with about 60% of diesel three-wheeler engines [44][6].

The products: the G435 A BS VI (435 cc, air-cooled, 5.6 kW) and G599 W BS VI (599 cc, water-cooled, 7 kW) for three-wheelers, and the G499 W Euro V+ (499 cc, 6.0 kW), billed as the world's first single-cylinder EU5+ L6eB diesel [47][48][49]. Single-cylinder means one piston, which keeps cost and weight low (about 59-64 kg). CNG engines, which run on compressed natural gas, are a small share [62]. Engines are built at the Chikalthana and Shendra units in CSN, and a dual-conveyor line was added in FY26 for capacity [6][26].

Delivery is to OEM assembly lines under multi-year contracts that index raw materials “but it comes with a lag” [24]. Price per engine is not disclosed; cost pass-through from Q4 FY27 is expected [24]. Spares reach owners through the Greaves retail network of 200+ distributors, 20,000+ mechanics and 7,000+ retailers [6]. Auto-engine revenue grew 48% in Q4 FY26 and 37% in Q2 FY27, though the CEO said the shift to CNG and electric has been “more gradual than we expected” [26][24][27].

web_blocks.title: Example 3, Mobility Solutions: Excel's push-pull cable and gear-shift lever
paragraphs: A push-pull cable is a steel wire inside a flexible sheath that carries a push or a pull from a driver's lever to a throttle, brake or gearbox. Excel's buyers are commercial-vehicle, construction-equipment, agricultural, marine and rail makers. Named wins include Stanley Black & Decker (a best-process-control award in January 2026), CAT (UK) and TAFE in Q1 FY27 and Tata Motors' international business in Q2 FY27 [3][1][42].

Excel makes cables, mechanical and electronic gear-shift and throttle levers, conduits and sensors in Nagpur, with a new conveyorised cable-assembly line commissioned in FY26 [6][26]. It is shifting from standalone parts to complete assemblies [6]. In FY22, before Greaves bought in, it earned ₹36.7 crore of profit before tax on ₹166.5 crore of turnover, with about 40% exported [38]. In FY26 its statutory segment result was ₹53.75 crore on ₹252.06 crore, 21.3% before central costs [6]. Billing terms and prices are not disclosed.

web_blocks.title: Example 4, Industrial Solutions: a certified fire-pump engine
paragraphs: A fire pump must reach rated pressure and flow at once. Global buyers want engines with FM and UL listings (independent safety certifications), which management says “very few companies in the world” hold [24]. Greaves sells to fire-pump makers and channel partners at home and abroad, to the armed forces directly, to marine and fishing-boat builders, and to agricultural makers of power tillers, mini tractors and pumps [26][25][1].

The range runs from the 3G11, 4G11 and 6G11 and D3V6 and D3V8 series at 30-750 HP, including a 750 HP fire engine launched in Q2 FY27, down to air-cooled 1-20 HP engines for tillers and sprayers [50][51][1]. Greaves cites over 20,000 fire engines deployed [50]. Exports of FM-UL engines started in Q1 FY27, and a global firefighting-equipment maker wrote a letter of appreciation in Q4 FY26 [24][26]. Per-unit prices are not disclosed. The annual report flags a volume decline at a major OEM, farm-price pressure and state orders linked to subsidies as risks to this segment [6].

web_blocks.title: Example 5, Investee: an Ampere electric scooter and an L5 three-wheeler
paragraphs: The buyer is a value-segment rider moving from a petrol scooter on running cost, or a fleet: a food-service major runs 20,000+ Ampere units, and e-commerce channels were about 13% of GEML retails [1]. The Nexus EX+ sells at ₹1,29,999 (₹1,35,999 with Intellipack connectivity) with a 5 kW motor, and the Magnus G-Max with Intellipack at ₹1,09,999 with a 142 km range on the Indian Driving Cycle. The whole range uses LFP batteries (lithium iron phosphate, a safer, nickel-free chemistry) [1][6]. Batteries carry a 60-month, 75,000 km warranty on current models [98].

GEML builds at Ranipet, with capacity of 4,80,000 units a year and about 40% utilisation in Q2 FY27, and sells through 418 dealers (320 a year earlier) [1]. The PM E-DRIVE scheme pays ₹2,500 per kWh, capped at ₹5,000 per vehicle, on e-2Ws up to ₹1.5 lakh ex-factory [57], about 3.8% of the Nexus EX+ price (our arithmetic). L5 vehicles are made by MLR Auto at Toopran (18,000 a year), with a financing tie-up offering up to 95% of the vehicle value [6]. L5 diesel share was 4.2% in Q2 FY27 [1].

web_blocks.title: Example 6, Investee: a loan from Greaves Finance
paragraphs: A driver or rider who cannot pay cash applies to GFL (ev.fin), which lends against electric two- and three-wheelers of any brand; approval takes “under 2.5 minutes” [6]. Managed assets were ₹630 crore at September 2026 (₹521 crore in March 2026) across 11 manufacturers [1][4]. GFL funds the book with debt, including ₹185 crore of 10.5% secured debentures in H1 FY27, and is rated IND A- (Stable) [2][6]. Its FY26 revenue was ₹39 crore and its own accounts show a profit of ₹1.57 crore against a ₹7.99 crore loss; the statutory segment shows a ₹4.74 crore loss, and the filings do not reconcile the two [4][6][2].

web_blocks.caption: Per-unit economics: what the filings disclose and what they do not
rows: Net revenue per unit ₹93,100 (₹85,100 a year earlier); EBITDA per unit -₹6,300 (-₹20,000) [1]
Cost split per unit; battery cost
Up to ₹5,000 per vehicle, about 5.4% of ex-factory realisation (our arithmetic) [57][1]
Dealers 418; 18 to 25 units per dealer per month; about 40% of 40,000 units a month of capacity [1][24]
Price per kVA, dealer margin, service revenue share
Units, price per engine, customer shares
web_blocks.takeaway: Only GEML gives true per-unit economics, and they show a business still losing money on each scooter but roughly 70% less than a year ago [1]. For the core, you must infer the economics from segment margins: about 17% for Engines and 21% for Excel before central costs, and 14.4% core EBITDA [6][4]. Unit prices, volumes and customer shares for the businesses that earn the profit are not in the filings.

web_blocks.title: What the filings do not disclose
paragraphs: Profit by Energy, Mobility and Industrial; prices or volumes for gensets, three-wheeler engines, Excel parts and fire engines; the revenue share of any customer; installed engine and genset capacity; the genset order book; and customer names beyond a handful. The annual report says “there is no single customer dependency”, and the top five debtors were 19% of trade receivables [6]. About 48% of sales go through dealers and distributors, down from 55% [6]. These gaps matter because the biggest uncertainty about the core sits exactly where disclosure is thinnest.

web_blocks.title: What this means for an owner
paragraphs: Our independent read is that Greaves's earnings power sits in Engines and Excel, which show 17-21% segment margins, while the fastest growth sits in loss-making investees. The core businesses are growing (+20% in H1 FY27) yet earning a thinner margin, so the quality of that growth depends on how fast higher costs reach customer prices. The three-wheeler diesel line is the largest single exposure, at 15.8% of group revenue, in a market the rating agency calls shrinking [3][70]. Next, Chapter 3 follows the product from plant to buyer and tests whether the unit economics hold.

book_paragraphs: Imagine five customers on one ordinary working day. A hospital administrator signs for a diesel generator so the operating theatres never go dark. A three-wheeler assembly line drops an engine into the frame of a cargo rickshaw. A Nagpur workshop wraps a steel cable for an equipment maker abroad. A fire-pump maker tests an engine that must roar to full pressure in seconds. A delivery rider in Patna rolls an electric scooter out of a showroom. You and I would call those five separate worlds. Greaves calls them one company, and your job in this chapter is to see how the pieces fit.

Warren Buffett said that “risk comes from not knowing what you're doing.” With Greaves that is harder than it sounds, because the company describes itself in two languages. Management speaks of three core segments, Energy, Mobility and Industrial, plus two investee businesses. The accountants, following a rule called Ind AS 108, report different segments, the ones the CEO and CFO actually review. In FY26 the three core segments brought in ₹742 crore, ₹1,584 crore and ₹339 crore, which is 28%, 59% and 13% of the ₹2,665 crore core. Next to them sit the electric two-wheeler maker GEML with ₹786 crore and the vehicle lender GFL with ₹39 crore. Both views are right. Neither tells you the profit of each of the three core segments, and that is the first thing the company does not say.

Here is what the accountants' view adds. Their biggest segment, Engines, brought in ₹2,241.39 crore of FY26 revenue and earned a segment result of ₹376.59 crore, a margin of 16.8%. Excel's cable segment earned 21.3% on ₹252.06 crore. The electric segment lost ₹182.01 crore on ₹786.19 crore. Take off central costs of ₹85.78 crore, finance costs and a ₹39.34 crore exceptional charge, and profit before tax was ₹114.91 crore. Tax of ₹79.62 crore then took most of it, leaving ₹35.29 crore. Hold on to the pattern: two segments produce the profit, and one takes a large part of it back.

Start with Energy, the segment you can picture most easily. A genset is a diesel engine bolted to an alternator, a machine that turns fuel into electricity when the grid fails or does not reach. kVA tells you how much electrical load it can carry; a 250 kVA set is about 200 kW, enough for a small factory or a clinic. Greaves makes sets from 5 to 2,500 kVA. The group it calls MHP, medium horsepower, covers 160 to 750 kVA, and the CEO told investors, “Our medium horsepower, which we call MHP genset portfolio, covering the 160 to 750 kVA range, grew 35% during the first half of FY27 compared to a 28% growth of the overall business.” That outperformance matters because MHP is where Greaves is trying to take share from larger rivals. Management puts its share at around 4%, so there is a lot of room and a lot of competition.

Why does a customer choose one genset over another? Less than you may think about the engine and more about who answers the phone when it stops. That is why Greaves sells through dealers who handle sales, service and spares, and why it offers a five-year extended warranty. The largest single order it has won, ₹35 crore, covers supply, installation, commissioning and long-term maintenance. Think of it like buying a lift for a building: the box is the beginning, and the contract for keeping it running is the lasting relationship. Aftermarket sales, which means spares and service, rose 35% in FY26.

Mobility is the biggest piece, and the engine in a three-wheeler is its heart. These are single-cylinder diesel engines of 435 to 599 cc, about 60 kg each. They are simple and low-cost, which is the point: an auto-rickshaw owner counts every rupee of running cost. Greaves says it makes about 60% of diesel three-wheeler engines in India. A newer version, the 499 cc Euro V+, goes into French microcars, the tiny quadricycles you see in European city centres, and Greaves is the sole engine supplier to that customer, Ligier. Management admitted on the Q2 FY27 call that its contracts with vehicle makers index raw-material costs “but it comes with a lag.” Read that carefully: when aluminium and copper rise, Greaves pays first and recovers later.

There is a bigger worry hiding in this line. Three-wheeler diesel engines brought in ₹545 crore in FY26, 15.8% of group revenue. India Ratings has called that industry “continuously shrinking,” and in February 2026 the CEO said the shift to CNG and electric vehicles had been “more gradual than we expected.” Both statements can be true: a slowly shrinking market can still grow for a leader who gains share, which is what auto-engine revenue growth of 37% in Q2 FY27 suggests. But a business whose market is slowly closing is one you should study with care.

Costs are the next thing to understand. Engines and gensets are made mostly of metal, and in October 2026 the CFO named the buckets: aluminium, iron, copper and platinum-group metals, which are used in exhaust catalysts. Core raw-material cost rose from 63.9% of core revenue in H1 FY26 to 67.8% in H1 FY27, and core EBITDA margin fell from 14.9% to 12.0%. The CEO said, “The improvement in margins has been slower than we had anticipated.” Management expects customer contracts to catch up from the fourth quarter of FY27. Until then Greaves does the same work and keeps less of each rupee.

The other big Mobility piece is Excel Controlinkage, and its product is wonderfully plain. A push-pull cable is a steel wire inside a flexible sheath. Pull a lever and the wire pulls a throttle or a brake at the other end; push it and the wire pushes. Tractors, excavators, boats and trucks all use them. Excel makes the cables, the gear-shift levers, conduits and sensors, and it is moving to sell whole assemblies. Its history shows good economics: ₹36.7 crore of pre-tax profit on ₹166.5 crore of FY22 turnover, and a segment result of 21.3% on ₹252.06 crore in FY26. Greaves now owns all of it.

Industrial Solutions is the smallest segment, at 13% of core, and the most specialised. Its best-known product is the fire-pump engine. A fire pump has to deliver rated pressure the instant it starts, and global buyers insist on engines certified by FM and UL, two safety bodies. Management says “very few companies in the world” hold those listings. In the second quarter of FY27 Greaves launched a 750 HP version. The segment fell 5% in H1 FY27 on paper, because Greaves exited finished farm machines, which Chinese imports had made very competitive. Strip that out and the rest grew 9%. Exiting a bad business to protect a good one is not a retreat; it is housekeeping.

Now the part that moves the group's results most: the investees. GEML makes Ampere electric scooters. In the latest quarter it earned ₹93,100 of net revenue per scooter and lost ₹6,300 of EBITDA per scooter, down from a loss of ₹20,000 a year earlier. Vikas Singh, GEML's MD, said, “Dealer throughput has improved by almost 40% year-on-year per dealer, from 18 to 25 units per month.” The factory at Ranipet can make about 40,000 a month and runs at about 40%. A scooter at ₹1,29,999 gets up to ₹5,000 from the PM E-DRIVE subsidy, around 4% of its price. Charlie Munger said, “Show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome.” Remember September 2023, when the incentive was taken away and volume fell 56%. GFL, the lender next door, now manages ₹630 crore of loans, which supports its customers' purchases and adds to the group's debt.

One more vehicle belongs to the investee story. L5 is the official class of full-size three-wheelers, the auto-rickshaws and small cargo carriers you see in every Indian town. GEML's MLR Auto builds electric and diesel versions at Toopran in Telangana, with capacity of 18,000 a year, and one electric model set an India Book of Records mark of 324 km on a single charge. Its diesel L5 share was 4.2% in Q2 FY27. Here too the government mattered: PM E-DRIVE support for electric L5 vehicles closed on 26 December 2025 when its funds ran out, so buyers now decide without it.

Look at the places where we simply cannot see. The filings give no price for a genset, an engine, a cable or a fire pump. They give no volumes and no customer shares beyond a statement that no customer dominates. They do not say how much of Energy's revenue is service. They do not give the genset order book. When you meet a gap like this, there are two sane responses: assume the worst or ask for more. We recommend the second, and in the chapters ahead we flag each gap where it matters.

Now weigh the mix both ways. The bull reading says Energy grew 20% in FY26 and 28% in H1 FY27, auto engines grew 37% in Q2, Excel grew 30%, GEML's revenue doubled, and the core holds ₹110 crore of net cash. The bear reading says the core margin fell nearly three percentage points in a year, Industrial is flat to down, Excel shrank in FY26, the diesel three-wheeler market is shrinking, and GEML has never earned an operating profit. We lean on the first reading for revenue and the second for margin. The mix is getting bigger faster than it is getting richer.

One last detail on where the money comes from. Overseas sales were ₹343.93 crore in FY26, 10.0% of the statutory total and up almost 73% on the year, and management's own measure of international share is 13% of core revenue. Customers sit in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Nepal and the United States. Ninety percent of the group's revenue is still earned in India, so Indian rules on emissions, subsidies and monsoons matter more to Greaves than any foreign factor.

So here is the summary you can carry. The core businesses, Energy, Mobility and Industrial, earn healthy margins on engines and cables and are growing at 16-20%. The investees grow faster and lose money. The data about each core segment's profit and each product's price is missing. In the next chapter we follow a product from plant to customer and ask whether Greaves keeps enough of every rupee.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A business description that only lists products tells you what a company makes. A good one tells you who pays, why, and what keeps them paying. Greaves answers the second part well for gensets and fire engines, where service and certification hold the customer, and less well for the diesel three-wheeler engine, where the customer base is shrinking.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The most useful number in this chapter is a loss: ₹6,300 per scooter. It is small enough to be hopeful and large enough to remind you that the group's best-growing business has not yet earned its keep. Follow that figure each quarter.
